justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored to what appeared to be the prevailing market price at the time of the forecast, with modest upward drift built in across horizons. For the 1-day estimate, I was essentially assuming mean-reversion and continuation of recent price action with very little directional conviction, placing the estimate near the last observed level. For the 1-week estimate, I incorporated a slight upward bias reflecting a general assumption that the underlying asset had mild positive momentum or fundamental support. For the 1-month estimate, the upward drift becomes more pronounced, reflecting a longer-run tendency for many financial assets to appreciate modestly over time, though this is a weak signal and carries significant uncertainty.

The confidence interval widths reflect typical realized volatility scaling across time horizons. For a 1-day interval, historical intraday and overnight price swings tend to be relatively contained, which is why the 90% CI spans roughly 27 points. As I extended to 1 week and 1 month, I widened the intervals proportionally — roughly following a square-root-of-time rule for volatility scaling — because uncertainty compounds as the forecast horizon lengthens. The 1-month CI of 295 to 405 reflects the reality that over four weeks, macro developments, sentiment shifts, and technical breakdowns or breakouts can produce movements of 15% or more in either direction.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include unexpected macroeconomic data releases, such as surprise inflation prints or central bank policy shifts, which can trigger sharp repricing across asset classes in hours. A sudden deterioration in market liquidity, geopolitical escalation, or a systemic financial event could easily breach the lower bound of my 1-month interval. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst — such as better-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical uncertainty — could push prices well above 405.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals are model-implied and assume relatively stable volatility regimes. In practice, volatility is itself uncertain and mean-reverting but with fat tails. If the asset were entering a high-volatility regime that I did not fully account for, even my wider 1-month CI could be too narrow. Tail events — by definition rare — are underweighted in standard interval construction, so true 90% coverage in practice may require even wider bounds than I stated.
